about: The wire contract of the secrets broker's RFC 8693 token exchange, as its two clients speak it: the Go client of packages/envoy/internal/brokerclient and the TypeScript client of packages/broker-client.
Each suite reads this one file and replays every exchange below against a stub broker of its own, so neither client's idea of the contract is only its own.

The rule that makes 'one contract' checkable rather than asserted: form, proof.header and proof.claims are the WHOLE of what a request carries. A suite asserts set equality, not containment, so a field one client starts sending without an entry here fails that client's own test, and a field added here fails the other client's test until it sends it too. expect.token is read the same way: it is the whole of what a client may take from an answer, so a client that starts reading another member of the answer fails until this file names it.
A value of the form ${name} is a placeholder each suite substitutes or checks by shape; placeholders names them. Everything else is literal and compared byte for byte.

There is no audience parameter: the broker's exchange has none. A subject token's own audience is what names the broker it may be spent at (BROKER_EXCHANGE_K8S_AUDIENCE, BROKER_GOOGLE_OIDC_AUDIENCE, BROKER_SIGNIN_DEVICE_AUDIENCE), and a client that posted one would be posting a field the broker does not read.

placeholders.${subject_token}: the token the exchange's subject source answered at this trade
placeholders.${actor_token}: the token the actor source answered at this trade
placeholders.${session}: the session name the client was configured with, as the entry's session names it
placeholders.${token_endpoint}: the stub broker's own origin followed by endpoint.path, with no query and no fragment
placeholders.${jti}: a value this request alone carries: non-empty, and never equal to another request's
placeholders.${iat}: the time the proof was signed, in whole seconds, within a minute of the suite's clock
placeholders.${public_jwk}: the public half of the client's own key: an EC P-256 JWK carrying x and y and no d member at all

exchanges.name: a pod trades its projected Kubernetes service-account token
exchanges.about: The identity a pod already holds, read from the file its runtime mounts and read again at every renewal, since the kubelet rewrites it in place.

exchanges.name: a machine trades its Google identity token
exchanges.about: A Compute Engine machine's own identity token, asked of its metadata server with format=full and fetched through no proxy. An entry that fixes the session leaves the client naming none.

exchanges.name: a person trades their sign-in with the machine as the actor
exchanges.about: The one request that carries two tokens: the person's own Google identity token from the device grant, and the machine's as the actor token, under a type of its own because what it proves is which box the person is asking from.

exchanges.name: the broker refuses the identity
exchanges.about: An identity no entry lists, a revoked sign-in, a token of the wrong audience: a refusal no retry can cure. The client stops with a plain error carrying what the broker said, and holds no token.

body.error_description: no entry lists the account this token names

expect.error_contains: no entry lists the account this token names

exchanges.name: an answer that carries a refresh token
exchanges.about: This grant issues none: a renewal is a fresh subject token traded again. A client that kept one would hold a credential the contract says is never minted, so an answer carrying one is refused.

exchanges.name: an answer of a token type that is not DPoP
exchanges.about: Every token this grant mints is bound to the key the caller proved. A bearer token would be one a copy of the answer could spend, so the client refuses it rather than presenting it.
